newsitem.title: POLAND: Big names' boost to Bank Handlowy sale seen modest.
newsitem.headline: Big names' boost to Bank Handlowy sale seen modest.

text.p: Poland's Bank Handlowy SA may benefit from having three top foreign financial institutions as stockholders but it will have only limited impact on the bank's public offer, analysts said on Friday.

By Thursday the U.S. bank JP Morgan, Swedish retail bank Swedbank and Swiss insurer Zurich Group had confirmed they were in talks with the Polish government over taking substantial stakes in Handlowy.

As part of Poland's biggest-ever privatisation, the three would take up to a 42.86 percent of the existing 65 million shares, representing up to 30 percent of Handlowy equity diluted by its convertible bond issue.

Aside from this so-called stable investor tranche, another 45 percent of existing shares are on sale from May 26 to June 13 in a public subscription for domestic retail players and Polish and foreign institutions.

Analysts said the foreign partners would give more credibility to Handlowy's plans to expand outside its core corporate banking area which is seen as most exposed to pressure from foreign competition and shrinking margins.
But they said it was still far from clear how much impact the three foreign investors would have, and how soon, given their limited investment.

"In itself, the idea of bringing in an investment bank, a retail bank and an insurer is very good...but the big question is how big will those partners' real involvement be," said Artur Szeski, analyst at Bank Pekao SA brokerage.
He said that developing the retail network was costly and time consuming and would require not only a transfer of know-how but also significant spending.

Some analysts said it was still an open question whether the group and the government would agree on a price that would be acceptable for all three partners and how it would compare with the 28-35 zloty ($10.94) range set for the public offer.

"Given the way the role of stable investors is defined, we should expect a discount because they are to contribute their know-how without gaining control over the bank," said Andrzej Soldek, banking analyst at ING BSK Asset Management.
Under the draft agreement the group of investors would have to keep Handlowy shares for 18 months and be subject to certain restrictions for a further 18 months.
Soldek said a price lower than that set for the public offer in book-building for institutional investors could have a dampening effect on local retail investors.

But analysts said the privatisation of the bank, valued at 2.6-3.26 billion zlotys, would have greatest appeal to foreign institutions anyway and small local players might find it hard to digest the 341-million zloty retail offer.

"I don't think there will be much interest in Poland as the domestic investor goes after quick profits and here no-one is promising a 50 percent premium on bourse debut," said Pawel Tarnowski of Raiffeisen Capital & Investment Polska.
"But for a foreign player the stock's liquidity will be just as important as being in good company (with the stable investors)," he added.
Analysts said the offering might have more appeal to mainstream institutional investors such as pension funds than more specialised players dedicated to the region.

Bank Handlowy, however, has stressed its determination to lure small savers not only to guarantee that Poland's oldest financial institution stays in Polish hands but also to build a potential customer base for its retail expansion.

Analysts said the strategy might help attract conservative individual investors but were sceptical whether Handlowy's ambition of gaining 200,000 small shareholders was realistic. ($ = 3.198 Polish Zlotys)
